talks.title: Flipping Bits: Your Credentials Are Certainly Mine
talks.teaser: STÖK analyzes Flipping Bits: Your Credentials Are Certainly Mine.
talks.summary:
Overview: Did you know that if you change a single bit from 1 to 0 (or vice versa) in the first 'g' of the domain name google.com (which is 01100111 in binary) you will end up with variety of valid "bitflip" domains like coogle.com, oogle.com, & woogle.com

So what happens if you generate and register a bunch of cheap bitfliped versions of popular cloud / Saas provider domains, point them to your VPS, log all incoming requests & then forget about the whole thing for two years?

Well you will in fact receive a stiff bill, generate huge log files and eventually run out of disk space. But on the upside, yo
Details: u will also have collected a treasure trove of legit credentials & interesting stuff like valid OAuth refresh tokens, JWT tokens, bearers, cookies, emails, meeting invites with passwords & truckloads of internet scanner noise.

In this session we will revisit bitflip research from the last decade and weponize it. Showcase 'Certainly' a pioneering offensive / defensive tool that employs Wildcard DNS matching & on-the-fly generated SSL certificates and custom payloads for incoming requests across various protocols. All with the intention to downgrade security, harvest credentials, capture emails and replacing dependencies with custom "malicious" payloads

talks.title: Advanced Fuzzing With LibAFL
talks.teaser: Shows how the LibAFL fuzzing library drives coverage-guided fuzzing across binaries, emulators and many cores.
talks.summary:
Fuzzing runs a target repeatedly with altered inputs and keeps the inputs that reach new coverage. The talk introduces LibAFL, a Rust fuzzing library, and compares executor designs such as fork servers, in-process harnesses and library-style calls, along with their speed and reproducibility trade-offs. It also covers mutators that go beyond random byte changes, including token-based, structure-aware and grammar-based mutation, and comparison logging that splits multi-byte checks into steps the fuzzer can solve one at a time.

For targets without source code, the talk covers binary instrumentation with QEMU, Frida and TinyInst, and what each costs in platform support and overhead. A worked example fuzzes a Samsung image codec on a Linux host by loading an Android library into QEMU user mode, stubbing system calls so the code runs without kernel interaction, and using snapshot resets with AddressSanitizer to catch a heap out-of-bounds write. Scaling is covered next: a shared-memory broker lets many cores exchange test cases, avoiding the kernel contention that stalls classic AFL beyond about 25 cores.

The closing section looks at fuzzing for injection flaws by hooking query functions and flagging inputs that reach them, and at future directions such as fuzzing web servers through REST grammars and using language models to suggest assertions or inputs. The main takeaway is that a fuzzer can be pointed at almost any target if the harness and instrumentation are built with care.

talks.title: Make ATM Jackpotting Great Again, the Ocelot way! - Jesus Dominguez y Bryan Enrique Gonzalez Velez
talks.teaser: Shows how an offensive team pairs PCILeech DMA with custom kernel modules to drive an ATM's cash dispenser through XFS.
talks.summary:
The Ocelot team from Metabase Q, an offensive security research group, walks through building a lab ATM for jackpotting research. They explain how to choose a model with accessible vault, fascia and BIOS, and why the bank's encrypted deployment image and the vault-gated dispenser synchronization make the old hard-drive-swap attacks harder. The middle of the talk covers the XFS API that controls the cash dispenser, including the info and execute commands malware uses to count notes per cassette, the per-transaction note limit, and a cassette fault that was cleared with the exchange commands.

To get code onto a machine with USB and SATA ports disabled, the team uses PCILeech, a DMA tool that reads and writes memory over PCI Express without installed drivers. They load a kernel module that patches a function in the Windows kernel to run a command loop, then build a module that receives shellcode in chunks larger than the tool's 4 KB limit and injects it into a 32-bit process. An EDR blocked injection into Notepad, so they describe two bypasses: renaming the EDR executables and their parent process, and injecting into a whitelisted 32-bit vendor binary on the ATM.

A recorded lab demonstration shows the sequence from booting the ATM to dispensing notes. The speakers close by noting that a whitelisted process should not be able to touch the dispenser when the security solution is properly configured, which points defenders toward restricting which processes can reach XFS services and protecting endpoint agents from tampering.

talks.title: Facebook Messenger Bug Hunting - A Bug's E2E Lifecycle -Samuel Cohen y Luke McLaren
talks.teaser: Walks through Messenger bug bounty findings, from a branded-link spoof to client-side crashes found by fuzzing native code.
talks.summary:
The speakers introduce Meta's bug bounty program, which they describe as a final safeguard after internal reviews and automated tooling. Rewards follow the company's own impact guidelines rather than CVSS, and a loyalty program called Hacker Plus adds bonus multipliers and invitations. They then outline Messenger's clients and its native libraries, noting that end-to-end encryption introduced in late 2023 pushed much of the message validation onto the client.

The first case is a branding flaw. A check for a Threads domain matched any host that merely contained that string, so crafted links appeared as Threads links inside encrypted chats. It paid a $1,000 base. Next, AR effect payloads carry a URL that a native validator checks. Memory-corruption fuzzing found nothing, so the speaker fuzzed the validator's logic instead, comparing its verdicts with the domain they expected. After about 44 million iterations, 13 unexpected inputs appeared, and one malformed URL repeatedly crashed a receiving Android client, a low-impact issue. Separately, negative offsets in mention and word effect data crashed recipients' clients, leaving affected group chats unusable. Two such reports paid a $3,000 base each.

The talk shows how edge-case features in large messaging apps widen the attack surface, and how payouts weigh realistic user impact as much as technical difficulty. The fixes were typically simple, such as adding delimiters or bounds checks.

talks.title: Breaking corporate Maven repositories
talks.teaser: Michael Stepankin investigates Breaking corporate Maven repositories.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Michael Stepankin, a security researcher at GitHub Security Lab, details his investigation into vulnerabilities within popular Maven repository managers and corporate artifact stores. Prompted by an initial arbitrary file read discovery on search.maven.org years earlier, Stepankin focused on the centralized nature of Maven Central and enterprise artifact proxies. Because major tech companies ingest dependencies through Maven repositories, compromising an upstream or internal repository manager provides an avenue to alter software supply chains. By auditing open-source repository engines like Sonatype Nexus (Nexus 2 and Nexus 3), JFrog Artifactory, and Reposilite, he identified multiple pre-authentication vulnerabilities that stem from proxying functionality, URL parsing differences, archive extraction, and metadata handling.

### Key Topics
- **Maven Ecosystem and Proxy Repositories**: How Maven resolves dependencies declared in `pom.xml` via group ID, artifact ID, and version, downloading artifacts (`.jar` and `.pom` files) and storing them locally. Corporate environments typically route requests through in-house repository proxies (e.g., Nexus, Artifactory) to manage private packages and cache external dependencies.
- **Attack Surface Expansion via Proxy Mode**: In-house proxy repositories significantly widen an application's attack surface. Even though administrative functions require authentication, proxy configurations trigger server-side archive extraction, XML parsing, local caching, and admin UI rendering in response to unauthenticated client requests.
- **Archive Handling and Injection Attacks**: Stored XSS, path traversal, and remote code execution (RCE) vectors via malicious packages pulled from external or upstream repositories into local managers.
- **Name Confusion and Cache Poisoning**: Inconsistencies in how different repository systems normalize paths, semicolons, and URL-encoded characters, allowing attackers to poison caches by substituting legitimate packages with arbitrary dependencies across package ecosystems (Maven, npm, Docker, RubyGems, Go).

### Technical Details
- **Reposilite & Nexus Stored XSS and Path Traversal**: By injecting JavaScript into artifact content or metadata rendered in the administrative console, Stepankin achieved stored XSS. In Reposilite, the admin token secret was located in `localStorage`. He also uncovered a Zip Slip/path traversal vulnerability where Reposilite automatically unpacked javadoc archives, allowing an attacker to write a `.jar` file directly into the `workspace/plugins` directory to achieve RCE upon restart. An additional path traversal flaw in javadoc file retrieval permitted downloading files outside target folders via URL encoding, exposing user credentials from Reposilite's default SQLite database (`sqlite-jdbc`).
- **Name Confusion via URL/Path Inconsistencies**: Stepankin identified that repository managers parse path parameters differently. While exploring URL-encoded separators (such as `#` and `?`), he found that a semicolon followed by path traversal sequences (`..;/`) exposed major parsing divergences: Nexus 2 treated the full path as an artifact name with an enlarged group ID; Nexus 3 normalized paths first and consumed traversal segments; and JFrog Artifactory treated characters following a semicolon as path parameters. 
- **JFrog Artifactory Cache Poisoning Proof-of-Concept**: When Artifactory requested an artifact from an upstream server (such as an Apache snapshots repository running Nexus 2 behind Cloudflare), the upstream returned a different artifact than Artifactory mapped. As a demonstration, Stepankin targeted npm packages on Artifactory by requesting `is-even` combined with path traversal targeting `is-odd`. Artifactory accepted the response and poisoned its internal cache, delivering `is-odd` whenever clients requested `is-even`. JFrog upgraded this finding to critical and awarded a $5,000 bounty (which was donated to cancer research).
- **Parameter Manipulation & Nexus 2 RCE**: Artifactory supported special query and matrix parameters, including `remoteSiteUrl`, which could theoretically redirect upstream proxy destinations if smuggled. In Nexus 2, artifacts and internal metadata are stored directly on the file system rather than a database. Stepankin discovered an issue allowing access and manipulation of internal metadata files, escalating to remote code execution. He noted the Nexus 2 RCE can be mitigated by blocking double forward slashes (`//`) in requests.

### Takeaways
Proxy modes in enterprise repository managers can expose internal networks to pre-authentication exploits because unauthenticated client requests trigger complex server-side processing on external artifacts. Furthermore, inconsistent URL and path normalization across intermediary proxies and upstream repositories enables cache poisoning across multiple package ecosystems. In total, the research uncovered seven high-to-critical CVEs across tested repository platforms.

talks.title: Windows Hello abuse, the sequel
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows Hello for Business keys and primary refresh tokens in Entra ID can be phished, abused and used for persistence.
talks.summary:
Windows Hello for Business is Microsoft's passwordless sign-in for Entra ID. A private key sits in the device's TPM and is unlocked with a PIN or biometrics. The talk, a follow-up to earlier research, examines how that key lifecycle can be abused. Registering a new key normally requires a fresh MFA check and a token tied to a known device, and the speaker shows where those checks fall short.

Starting from phishing, the speaker shows that a victim's login can be turned into a registered device, a primary refresh token and a new key that keeps working after a password reset. With malware on a user's endpoint, the user-level key can sign requests without admin rights. Other cases include a timestamp that could be stretched to years before a server-side nonce fix, a remote desktop session to a machine without a TPM exposing a session key, and an older key derivation function that could be forced back in. That last weakness was reported to Microsoft, and the speaker says it was not fully fixed at the time. The hybrid key trust feature can also sync keys created in Entra into on-premises Active Directory, which opens a cloud-to-on-prem path.

The practical takeaway is that a password reset alone is not enough after a suspected account compromise, because attacker-added passwordless credentials stay valid. Defenders should review new keys and devices, and think carefully before syncing highly privileged on-premises accounts to the cloud. The tools used are open source.

talks.title: Project 0xA11C: Deoxidizing the Rust Malware Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Fishbein details Project 0xA11C: Deoxidizing the Rust Malware Ecosystem.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Oliver from Sentinel One presents Project 0xA11C, an effort to improve reverse engineering of Rust malware binaries. The talk addresses why modern compiled languages—particularly Rust—present severe challenges for security researchers and how increased tool sophistication is essential as malware developers adopt these languages.

## Key Topics
The presentation establishes context by discussing general issues with reverse engineering modern languages: massive statically-linked binaries, unconventional calling conventions, inadequate string handling in decompilers, poor type recovery, and inability to handle multiple return values. Oliver compares this to the Go reversing problem tackled previously through AlphaGolang, explaining why Rust presents fundamentally different challenges.

Rust's appeal to malware developers stems from its safety features, cross-platform compilation, active development, and the resulting difficulty analysts face when reversing it. The talk documents observed malware (Rust Bucket) and rewritten variants of previous Go/C malware now compiled to Rust.

## Technical Details
The project identifies several recoverable information sources in Rust binaries:

**Binary Identification & Metadata**: YARA rules identify Rust binaries. Rust version and commit hashes remain visible even in stripped binaries. Cargo dependency manager paths reveal library versions used during compilation.

**String and Slice Handling**: The team defines structures for immutable/mutable strings and slices (32/64-bit variants). Rust strings are sized and capacity-tracked rather than null-terminated, causing decompiler issues. Longer strings use XMM registers (sometimes reversed in hex representation), requiring script-based recovery.

**P Data Section Analysis (Windows)**: Symbols in P data organize by module/library with trait implementations and type functions. Exception handling information via unwinding structures indicates library functions (malware developers rarely implement exception handling, allowing user-defined function isolation from thousands of library functions). This reduces analysis scope from thousands to approximately 10-20 user functions.

**Panic Information Extraction**: Rust macros embed panic metadata (file paths, line numbers, column numbers) connecting binary offsets to source locations, providing sparse maps for identifying code relationships.

**Calling Conventions**: The problem space here involves IDA's inability to determine argument order and count when functions use arbitrary or custom calling conventions.

**Feature Proof Middleware**: A new library abstracting IDA Python implementation details across versions (6.8 through 9), preventing scripts from breaking with version updates. Community implementation in Binja and potential Ghidra support discussed.

**FLIRT Signatures**: Hex-Rays' approach in IDA 9 creates signatures for Rust versions and dependencies, allowing brute-force matching to recover library functions, traits, and generics.

## Takeaways
The project is on an extended timeline (originally 6 months, now 9+ months, likely 12+). Key conclusions: (1) Decompilers themselves require fundamental improvements for Rust beyond current tool capabilities; (2) Information recovery through binary analysis and script automation can reduce reversing scope but doesn't solve underlying decompiler problems; (3) Binary Ninja shows more promise than IDA Pro due to its intermediate abstraction architecture; (4) A community approach is essential, with multiple researchers attacking the same problems across different platforms; (5) Vast quantities of unanalyzed Rust malware exist because analysts avoid the difficulty; (6) VirusTotal integration enables large-scale Rust binary collection for heuristic development.

talks.title: LADO B
talks.teaser: Shows how learning-code car alarm remotes can be brute-forced over radio and how a tool automates the attack.
talks.summary:
This B-side compilation opens with a talk on car alarm remotes. The speaker began with a curiosity about why a pinball machine could not detect his car's 370 MHz keyfob signal. Captures showed the same unlock code repeating, which pointed to a learning-code alarm chip with roughly one million possible codes instead of a rolling code. By capturing the signal and reading the chip datasheet, he decoded the scheme: short pulses are zeros, long pulses are ones, and the 20-bit learning code and mode bits are sent in 4-bit groups. He then built a GNU Radio block to transmit candidate codes.

He wrote a brute-force tool that sends candidate codes with a set repeat count and delay, and tested it on parked cars in Quito. In one lot, three of four cars were vulnerable. He explained that the installer, not the dealer alone, determines the risk, since an aftermarket alarm can carry an extra code. He also demonstrated a scanner for finding hidden learning codes and a jamming-plus-replay option for rolling-code systems.

The rest of the compilation covers a MIFARE transit card analysis using an Android app and a Proxmark, where sector and token exchange findings were still a work in progress, plus interviews about the Latino Village at Ekoparty and the Future Hacker school outreach program. The practical takeaways are to prefer official alarms, insist on rolling codes, and push manufacturers to publish chip and security details.

talks.title: LADO B
talks.teaser: Offers a nearly nine-hour day-two stream from the Ekoparty Security Conference's 2024 event.
talks.summary:
This entry is the day-two recording of "LADO B," a stream published on the Ekoparty Security Conference YouTube channel as part of its 2024 event. The video was streamed live on November 14, 2024, and runs for about eight hours and fifty-two minutes. At capture time it had roughly 2,083 views, and the uploader left no written description.

The captured material contains only the page metadata, so the individual sessions, speakers, and topics inside the stream cannot be identified from it. The title is the only label tying the recording to the conference's day-two schedule. The other Ekoparty-branded videos listed alongside it are separate uploads, not segments of this one.

For a practitioner, the useful takeaway is limited. This is a long-form conference recording rather than a single presentation. Anyone looking for a specific talk should check the event's published schedule or the timestamps in the video itself before relying on it.
